title: Predict how by-value parameters and ref, out, or in affect caller storage

rubric.point: Calling the non-readonly Increment method through the readonly in parameter operates on a defensive copy of the struct, so its mutation does not reach the caller's storage.

questions.model: `counter.Value` remains `4`. Through the readonly `in` parameter, `Increment()` runs on a defensive copy of the struct, so only that copy changes.

c1.text: in makes param readonly, but it looks like we dont change the param value directly. Moreover we passing struct which is passed by a value, and in the method we just have a copy, so outer variable should not be changed

annotations.quote: outer variable should not be changed
annotations.note: You correctly concluded the caller's value stays 4.

annotations.quote: in makes param readonly, but it looks like we dont change the param value directly.
annotations.note: `Increment()` does mutate the struct. It is a non-readonly method, and calling it is exactly what triggers the defensive copy.

annotations.quote: in the method we just have a copy
annotations.note: An `in` parameter is passed by reference, not by value, so there is no up-front copy. The copy is made only at the `Increment()` call, because the parameter is readonly and the method is not.

c1.feedback: The prediction of 4 is right, but you attributed it to by-value copying instead of the defensive copy the compiler makes when a non-readonly method is called on an `in` parameter.
